lead: Software architecture is the set of early, large decisions about a system: its main parts, how those parts talk, where data lives, and what runs on which machine. A style is a named template for those decisions, such as layered or client-server. Architecture matters because it fixes the qualities that are hard to add later — performance, security, modifiability — and because every later design choice must fit inside it. Booking apps, banking systems and compilers all carry an architecture whether or not anyone named it.
prereq: You need: 3.2 on modules and decomposition, and Unit 2 on non-functional requirements.

sections.h3: Architecture is chosen early, then checked

blocks.text: A subsystem is a group of modules that does one part of the job. The architecture names those subsystems and the rules for how they may interact.

items: Take the structural elements from the requirements: use cases, data flow diagrams, entities, and the non-functional needs from Unit 2.
Group the elements into subsystems, using high cohesion and low coupling from 3.2.
Map the subsystems onto a named architectural style, or a mix of styles.
Check the result against the quality attributes: performance, security, availability, modifiability, testability. If a check fails, change the grouping or the style.

blocks.text: Architecture is fixed early because the cost of change grows with time. A wrong module boundary can be repaired in a week; a wrong choice of tiers may need new servers, new contracts and a new deployment plan. The style also sets what is easy. A layered system makes a new screen easy and a tight real-time loop hard. A pipe-filter system makes a new processing step easy and an interactive undo button hard.

Data design is part of the same early work. Entities from the requirements model become tables. A primary key is a column, or a small set of columns, that uniquely identifies one row. A foreign key is a column that points to a primary key in another table. Normalisation is the process of removing repeated data so that one fact is stored once; third normal form is a common target. Good data design reduces update errors and makes queries predictable.

items: Layered. Structure: code is grouped into layers. Each layer offers services to the layer above and uses the layer below. A layer is a logical group of code, not a machine. Helps: modifiability and testability, because a layer can be replaced if its interface stays. Hurts: performance, because a request may pass through several layers. Used in: enterprise web applications and business software.

Client-server. Structure: a client sends requests; a server holds shared data or services and sends replies. Helps: central control of data and security. Hurts: the server can become a bottleneck or a single point of failure. Used in: web applications, database-backed booking systems, and most network services.

Pipe-filter. Structure: a filter reads input, transforms it, and writes output. A pipe is a connector that carries data from one filter to the next. Helps: reuse and composition, because filters can be rearranged. Hurts: interactivity and latency, because data must flow through every stage. Used in: compilers, Unix-style command pipelines, and log or image processing.

blocks.text: Layer and tier are not synonyms. A layer is a logical group of code. A tier is a physical place where code runs. A design with three layers can be deployed in two tiers when the business-logic layer and the data-access layer run on one server.

Repository or blackboard style: components share one data store and read or write it as needed; it suits data-heavy, uncertain problems and gives weak control over flow. Event-driven style: components react to events instead of calling each other; it gives loose coupling but makes the overall flow hard to trace.

sections.h3: Case study: a seat-booking system on three tiers

blocks.text: Take a train seat-booking system. The requirements give these structural elements: a search screen, a seat map, a fare rule, a seat-lock rule, payment, ticket records, and train and seat data. Group the code into three layers — presentation, business logic and data access — and treat the database as the data tier that stores the tables.

The presentation layer holds screens and forms. The business-logic layer holds rules: a seat is locked for a few minutes during payment, a child fare is half the adult fare, and a cancellation is allowed only before departure. The data-access layer turns those rules into queries and maps rows to objects. The database is not a layer of code; it is the data tier, holding tables such as TRAIN, SEAT, BOOKING and PASSENGER, with primary keys and foreign keys.

Deploy this as three tiers: a browser or mobile app as the presentation tier; an application server running business logic and data access as the middle tier; and a database server as the data tier. The quality check matters. The seat-lock rule needs a transaction so two users cannot book the same seat. The layered split makes a new payment method easy to add in the business layer, and it lets a load balancer put two application servers behind the presentation tier. The cost is extra network hops, which is acceptable for a booking site but wrong for a fast in-memory game loop.

figure.caption: The business-logic layer is picked out because it holds the rules, such as the seat lock, that the other layers must not duplicate. The stack runs from the user side at the top to the data side at the bottom, ending in the database tier.

spec.aria: Three code layers stacked from the user side down to the data side, with the business logic layer picked out as the one carrying the rules, and the database tier shown at the bottom.

examples.question: A log pipeline has three filters. Parse takes 4 ms per record, validate takes 6 ms, and format takes 2 ms. Records arrive at 100 per second. (a) What is the steady-state throughput of the pipeline? (b) What is the latency of one record? (c) Where is the bottleneck, and what does a second copy of that filter buy?
steps: Convert each filter time to seconds: parse = 0.004 s, validate = 0.006 s, format = 0.002 s.
In steady state, a pipe-filter pipeline cannot process faster than its slowest filter. The slowest filter is validate at 0.006 s per record.

Capacity = 1 ÷ 0.006 s = 166.7 records per second. Arrivals are 100 per second, which is below capacity, so the pipeline is not saturated: steady-state throughput = 100 records per second (arrival-limited) and the queue stays bounded.
Latency of one record through an empty pipeline = 0.004 + 0.006 + 0.002 = 0.012 s = 12 ms. This is the minimum; under load a record also waits behind earlier records, so measured latency is higher.
The bottleneck is validate. Two copies of validate working in parallel give 2 ÷ 0.006 s = 333.3 records per second of capacity.
examples.answer: Capacity is about 166.7 records per second; actual throughput is 100 records per second because arrivals are slower. Latency through an empty pipeline is 12 ms, higher under load. The bottleneck is validate; a second validate filter raises capacity to about 333.3 records per second.
examples.check:
parse = 0.004
validate = 0.006
fmt = 0.002
arrival = 100
capacity = 1 / validate
throughput = min(arrival, capacity)
latency = parse + validate + fmt
parallel = 2 / validate
print(round(capacity, 1))
print(round(throughput, 1))
print(round(latency * 1000, 1))
print(round(parallel, 1))

traps: Treating layer and tier as synonyms. A layer is logical code grouping; a tier is a physical runtime or deployment place. A 3-layer design can be 2 tiers.

Saying pipe-filter throughput is the sum of filter times. Sum gives latency, not throughput. Throughput is set by the slowest stage: throughput of a stage with n parallel copies = n ÷ (time per record of one copy of the slowest stage).
Calling any client-server system a 2-tier system. The label depends on where presentation, business logic and data actually run, not on the fact that a client calls a server.
Assuming architecture cannot change. It is fixed early because change is costly, not because change is impossible.

quiz.q: Define a layer and a tier in one sentence each.
quiz.a: A layer is a logical group of code that offers services to the layer above and uses the layer below. A tier is a physical place where code runs, such as a browser, an application server or a database server.

quiz.q: Name the three main architectural styles covered in this chapter and give one use of each.
quiz.a: Layered: enterprise web applications. Client-server: database-backed booking or banking systems. Pipe-filter: compilers and log-processing pipelines.

quiz.q: Why does a pipe-filter pipeline's steady-state throughput depend on its slowest filter?
quiz.a: Each record must pass through every filter. The slowest filter takes the longest time per record, so it limits how many records can leave the pipeline per second. Faster filters wait or buffer output; they cannot make the slow stage faster.

quiz.q: A pipeline has filters taking 5 ms, 10 ms and 4 ms. Records arrive at 80 per second. Find throughput and latency.
quiz.a: Slowest stage = 10 ms = 0.010 s, so capacity = 1 ÷ 0.010 = 100 records/s. Arrivals are 80/s, below capacity, so steady-state throughput = 80 records/s. Latency through an empty pipeline = 5 + 10 + 4 = 19 ms, plus queueing under load.

quiz.q: In a 3-tier booking system, which tier should hold the seat-lock rule, and why?
quiz.a: The middle application tier, inside the business-logic layer. The seat lock is a business rule, not a screen detail and not a raw database query. Keeping it there lets all clients share one rule.

quiz.q: Explain how a 3-layer design can be deployed as 2 tiers.
quiz.a: Layers are logical. If the business-logic layer and the data-access layer run in the same server process, they form one physical tier. The presentation layer runs on the client, giving the second tier.

quiz.q: Give one quality attribute that the layered style hurts, and explain the mechanism.
quiz.a: Performance. A request may pass through several layers, adding calls and data conversion at each boundary; if those layers sit on different tiers, extra network hops are added as well.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry often splits the middle tier into small services, which is microservices, and moves pieces to managed cloud services, which is serverless. Event-driven and repository styles return in data pipelines and message queues. Architects now draw views with the C4 model and test qualities with fitness functions. Search next for microservices versus layered architecture, event-driven architecture, and architecture fitness functions.
